Background (published research, not about this person): %1$s Source: %2$s.

Weight and activity can each move the other. Over 20 years, young adults who stayed highly active gained less weight than those who stayed less active; in children, a genetic analysis placed a higher body mass index before lower activity.

In a 14-day study of people in couples who rated themselves six times a day, moments rated as more tense went with lower sexual interest and arousal at the same moment, and sex went with lower cortisol afterwards. It measured moments, not months.
In a mathematical model of adult metabolism, body weight follows a lasting change in the energy eaten slowly: about half of the way in a year.

In daily diaries of university students, nights of heavier drinking were followed by lower good mood and well-being the next day, and nights of light drinking were not; poorer sleep carried part of the link in one of the two studies.

Pooled daily diaries found that people drank no more often on days of stronger bad feeling, and more often and more heavily on days of stronger good feeling. Months of drinking set against months of feeling wound up were not what they measured.
Across laboratory studies of healthy volunteers, alcohol before bed shortened the time to fall asleep, deepened the first half of the night and broke up the second half.
In a daily diary of students, days with more drinks were days with more sex; it measured days, not months. The research is mixed.

Published findings point different ways. Across 24 studies of men, light to moderate drinking went with fewer reports of difficulty with erections and heavy drinking with no difference; in a daily diary of students, days with more drinks were days with more sex. The research is mixed.

208 adults, about three in four of them recruited for low mood, worry or both, rated their sleep and mood each day for six weeks: a poorer night went with lower mood the next day more strongly than a low mood went with a poorer night. In experiments, shortened or broken sleep lowered good feeling.
Across 154 experiments in healthy people, shortened, broken or missed sleep was followed by feeling more tense and on edge, and by less good feeling.

In 80 adults aged 21 to 40 with a body mass index of 25 to 30 who usually slept under six and a half hours, two weeks of sleeping about 1.2 hours longer at home went with about 270 kcal a day less energy taken in than in those who kept their usual sleep, worked out from energy spent and body stores rather than food records; across 11 studies that shortened sleep, energy eaten was about 385 kcal a day higher.
In 12 healthy sleepers, 400 mg of caffeine taken six hours before bed was followed by more than an hour less sleep, measured at home, than a placebo.

Pooling 67 studies that paired a movement sensor with ratings on a phone, people felt slightly more cheerful and energetic in the hours around being more active, and slightly less calm; the link ran both ways and was small.
Across 25 trials, each kilogram of weight lost went with blood pressure about 1 mmHg lower, systolic and diastolic.
Across 34 trials of four weeks or more, about 4.4 g less salt a day, which is about 1.7 g of sodium, went with systolic pressure about 4 mmHg lower and diastolic about 2 mmHg lower.

Across 36 trials, people who drank more than two drinks a day and about halved it had lower blood pressure, most of all those who drank six or more (systolic 5.5 and diastolic 4.0 mmHg lower); at two drinks a day or fewer, no difference was found.

Across 73 trials of walking programmes that lasted 15 weeks on average, at about 150 minutes a week, systolic pressure was about 4 mmHg lower than in people who did not take part, and diastolic about 2 mmHg lower, a less certain figure. The trials set minutes of walking, not a count of steps.

Across 23 studies, each further cigarette a day went with a resting pulse about 0.2 beats a minute higher among people who smoked, and a genetic analysis put the difference at about 7 beats a minute at 20 cigarettes a day.

Moderate drinkers had higher ALT and GGT than people who did not drink, and AST no different; in 32 patients who had been heavy drinkers and kept off alcohol for eight weeks, GGT fell by half about every 26 days, so a result carries weeks of drinking rather than days.

In trials comparing periods of drinking with periods without, HDL cholesterol was about 0.09 mmol/L higher while drinking, about 0.07 mmol/L at 90 to 210 g of alcohol a week and 0.14 mmol/L above 420 g, and triglycerides did not differ on average except above 420 g a week.
In a national survey, serum urate ran higher with each daily serving of beer or spirits, and not with wine.
In trials, structured aerobic exercise went with HDL cholesterol about 0.065 mmol/L higher; in trials of walking alone, HDL and triglycerides did not differ on average.

Across 70 studies of dieting, weight loss went with lower total and LDL cholesterol and triglycerides; in a survey of 2,164 adults, ALT and the other liver enzymes ran higher at a higher body mass index.
Across 37 trials, higher sugar intakes went with triglycerides about 0.11 mmol/L higher than lower intakes.
Across 84 feeding studies, each 1 per cent of food energy moved from saturated to polyunsaturated fat went with LDL cholesterol about 0.055 mmol/L lower.

The bands come from published guidelines and reference intervals, WHO, ADA, ESC/EAS and KDIGO among them, and the blood bands assume a fasting sample; the report for the doctor names the body behind a band on its Reference line where the app records one. A number outside a band is a reason to ask a clinician, never a diagnosis — and a single result is not a trend. Blood glucose is shared with Health Connect; the rest has no record type there and stays on this device. Units follow the metric/imperial setting in your profile, mmol/L or mg/dL, except where a sheet may print either of two units whose ranges overlap, as vitamin D’s nmol/L and ng/mL do: there the field asks which one the sheet printed.
What is usually looked at next
What clinicians usually look at next

Reference reading, the same for everybody, about what these panels hold and how they are usually read. It is not about your own results and nothing here is advice — only a healthcare professional who can see the whole picture can tell you what your figures mean.

Blood sugar is read from more than one figure because each answers a different question. A fasting sample is a snapshot; HbA1c reflects roughly the previous eight to twelve weeks and leans on the most recent of them. Practice does not usually settle anything on a single result — a diagnosis normally wants two, either two different tests on one sample or the same test repeated. Near the margins a repeat months later is the usual next step rather than anything more.

HbA1c stops being a reliable picture of blood sugar when red cells are not behaving normally: anaemia, iron status, haemoglobin variants, recent blood loss or transfusion, late pregnancy, advanced kidney disease. In those situations glucose readings carry more of the picture than the percentage does.

Insulin and the HOMA-IR calculation built from it are shown here as figures only. The printed range on insulin is a laboratory’s reference interval, and laboratory-utilisation guidance reserves the calculation for research rather than for reading somebody’s result by.

Cholesterol is one measurement made of several. Total cholesterol, LDL, HDL and the non-HDL figure derived from them describe different fractions, and the risk conversation has moved onto non-HDL and apolipoprotein B rather than any single number.

Before anything else is considered, practice looks at what else could be lifting the figures: thyroid function, blood sugar, alcohol, liver and kidney results. A raised thyroid-stimulating hormone and a raised LDL on the same sheet are known to travel together, and treating the first has been measured to move the second.

Lipoprotein(a) is largely inherited and is generally measured once in a lifetime rather than followed. The two units it is reported in do not convert reliably between assays, so a figure is read against the range printed beside it.

On diet, the controlled trials are about substitution rather than subtraction: replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fat moves the numbers, and replacing it with carbohydrate does not. Soluble fibre specifically — not total fibre — is the fraction those trials measured.

HDL falls during active weight loss and rises again once weight is stable, which is worth knowing before a mid-diet result is read as a setback.

Creatinine on its own says little without the estimated filtration rate calculated from it, and that estimate uses age and sex in its equation. The version used here is creatinine-only and carries no race term.

The single most important thing about a low filtration estimate is that one reading cannot tell a passing insult from a lasting change. Kidney guidance is explicit that chronicity is not assumed from one result: a minimum of three months separates the two questions, so a repeat after that interval is the ordinary next step. Urine albumin is the other half of the picture, entered with a urine sample as the albumin-to-creatinine ratio.

Urate above the reference range without symptoms is frequently left alone. The rheumatology guidance conditionally recommends against treating it in the absence of attacks, including alongside kidney or cardiovascular disease.

ALT and AST are enzymes, not a measurement of how the liver is working, and a single raised result is usually repeated before anything follows it. Where it is followed up, the usual first steps are a clarifying test — gamma-GT to say whether a raised alkaline phosphatase is coming from the liver at all — and a history.

The reference ranges most laboratories print are wider than the figures gastroenterology guidance describes as a true healthy normal, which is why an in-range result and a flagged one can both appear on the same sheet from different laboratories. The range printed beside your own result is the one that laboratory used.

A pattern where AST sits above ALT, alongside substantial weekly alcohol, is one the guidance names specifically. The familiar two-to-one ratio appears in its narrative rather than as a numbered recommendation, so it is a rule of thumb rather than a line.

One index calculated from figures on these sheets is FIB-4, which combines age, AST, ALT and the platelet count: age × AST ÷ (platelets × √ALT). Published cut-offs are 1.3 and 2.67, with 2.0 used in place of the lower one above 65, and it is described as having low accuracy under 35. It is set out here so it can be read about, and this app does not calculate it from anybody’s values.

A raised total bilirubin cannot be interpreted without the split into direct and indirect, which is a separate request.

Haemoglobin below the WHO thresholds — 130 g/L for men and 120 g/L for non-pregnant women, figures scoped to ages 15 to 65 — is where a blood count is usually read from. WHO states that no adjustment for race or ethnicity should be made. Above 65 the evidence for a threshold is thin, so the adult line is a rough guide rather than a boundary.

Which direction the investigation takes depends on cell size, which is on the count itself: small cells point at iron, large ones at B12, folate, thyroid, liver or alcohol, ordinary-sized ones somewhere else again.

Ferritin is where most of the difficulty lives. It rises with inflammation as well as with iron stores, so a figure taken during an infection can look reassuring when it is not — WHO suggests reading it against a higher figure when inflammation is present, and asks for two inflammation markers where this app holds one. Gastroenterology guidance also reads ferritin against a substantially higher figure in somebody who is anaemic than in somebody who is not.

Iron stores and haemoglobin recover on different clocks: haemoglobin moves within about four weeks, ferritin over three to six months. They are not usefully re-checked together.

Menstrual loss is the largest single modifiable driver of iron stores in anybody who menstruates, and it is one this app can see from your own cycle records.

CRP answers two quite different questions depending on how high it is. The low end, measured by a high-sensitivity assay, is used in cardiovascular risk discussion. Above about 10 mg/L the guidance stops treating it as a risk figure at all and looks for infection or inflammation instead — and a repeat is the usual step, because a single high reading during an illness says nothing about anybody’s baseline.\n\nCRP also moves enormously on its own. Its within-person variation has been measured at over forty per cent, which means two readings have to differ by roughly double before the difference is more than noise. A chest infection in the week of a blood draw explains more than any diet does, which is why nothing in this app tries to relate CRP to what you ate.

A raised thyroid-stimulating hormone with a normal free T4 is the commonest thyroid result there is, and European guidance describes repeating both — with thyroid peroxidase antibodies — after an interval of two to three months. A different and often-confused interval, six to eight weeks, belongs to checking somebody after starting or changing thyroid hormone, which is not the same thing.

Age matters here more than on most panels. The upper end of the population range climbs steadily with age: a figure that would be flagged at thirty sits inside the age-specific range for most people in their eighties, and the majority of older people whose result is flagged are in fact within it. The band this app uses widens above seventy for that reason.

In the oldest patients with mildly raised values, the guidance describes careful watching rather than starting treatment. Nothing here suggests stopping a medicine anybody is already taking — that is a conversation with the person who prescribed it.

Thyroid results are also worth reading beside the lipid panel, since the two are known to move together.

Vitamin D is read from 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the total of D2 and D3; where a sheet prints the two separately, the figure to copy is their sum. The band here is the Institute of Medicine’s from 2011: below 30 nmol/L (12 ng/mL) deficiency becomes a risk, 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL) meets the needs of nearly everybody, and above 125 nmol/L (50 ng/mL) is where it asked clinicians to be concerned about adverse effects. The Endocrine Society, whose 2011 guideline put the line for sufficiency at 30 ng/mL (75 nmol/L), found in its 2024 guideline no clear evidence defining an optimal level for preventing disease, and suggests against routine testing in the populations it considered. A laboratory’s printed range may still start at 30 ng/mL, and the figure follows the season and the sun as well as anything taken.

B12 is read against NICE’s 2024 lines: below 180 ng/L (133 pmol/L) confirms a deficiency, and 180 to 350 ng/L (133 to 258 pmol/L) is indeterminate. Where validated thresholds vary locally, NICE says to use the ones set by the laboratory doing the test, so the range printed on the sheet comes first. Supplements, a multivitamin included, raise the figure and can mask a deficiency, which is why NICE asks for blood to be taken before B12 is started.

Serum folate reflects recent intake: WHO notes that a single measurement cannot tell a passing dip in the diet from a lasting deficiency. Its lines — 10 nmol/L, and 6.8 nmol/L (3 ng/mL) for deficiency — were written for assessing populations rather than one person, and a high figure mostly reflects supplements or fortified food, so nothing here calls it high.

Only about 0.3 per cent of the body’s magnesium is in the serum, and the serum figure does not reflect the total, so a result inside 0.7–1.0 mmol/L does not rule out a low store.

Transferrin saturation sits on the blood-count panel beside ferritin. Below 20 per cent indicates iron restriction in gastroenterology guidance. The upper lines — above 45 per cent in women, above 50 per cent in men and after menopause — come from the European guideline on haemochromatosis, where they are read together with ferritin to recognise iron overload, not as a range for everybody. Iron taken in the day before the draw raises it, and laboratories such as Mayo Clinic’s ask for none in the 24 hours before.

Among men: in a survey of 7,648 US men, those who masturbated more tended to have somewhat less partnered sex, and how content they were with their sex life predicted masturbation better than how often they had sex. In 1,784 US men, masturbation went with wanting more partnered sex, not with how much they had.
Regnerus M et al. Arch Sex Behav 2017;46(7):2111-2121 (PMID 28341933); Herbenick D et al. Arch Sex Behav 2023;52(3):1317-1331 (PMID 36575264)
Among women: in surveys of 8,090 and 1,958 US women, those who masturbated more tended to have more partnered sex, not less; wanting more partnered sex also went with more masturbation.
Regnerus M et al. Arch Sex Behav 2017 (PMID 28341933); Herbenick D et al. Arch Sex Behav 2023 (PMID 36575264); Gerressu M et al. Arch Sex Behav 2008;37(2):266-278 (PMID 17333329)
